passages.t: ‘Who is like the LORD our God?’: the Hallel begins
passages.happening:
Psalm 113 begins and ends with “Hallelujah!”, ‘praise the LORD’. In between it calls God's servants to praise his name (verse 1). “Blessed be the name of the LORD both now and forevermore” (verse 2). His name is praised “From where the sun rises to where it sets” (verse 3), which means everywhere, east to west.

Then a question. “Who is like the LORD our God, the One enthroned on high?” (verse 5). He is so high that “He humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth” (verse 6). He has to stoop even to look at the sky.

And this high God stoops lower still. “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dump to seat them with nobles, with the princes of His people” (verses 7 and 8). The psalm ends with one more picture: “He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 113 opens a group of six psalms, 113 to 118, called the Hallel, from the Hebrew word for ‘praise’. The book page's part on the temple tells how they were sung at the great feasts. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, describes the Passover meal. It says part of the Hallel was sung before the meal, either Psalm 113 alone or 113 and 114, and the rest was finished after it, over the last cup of wine. How much of that was fixed in Jesus' day is not certain, but the custom is old.

‘The dump’ (verse 7) was the rubbish heap outside a town, where waste was burned. Beggars and outcasts sat there. To be lifted from the dump to a seat among princes was the biggest reversal a hearer could imagine.

The barren woman (verse 9) would be felt just as strongly. In that world a woman with no children carried grief and often shame. Israel's story is full of such women whom God remembered: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah.

This psalm sounds very like Hannah's song after Samuel was born. She sang that God “raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap” (1 Samuel 2:8), and that “The barren woman gives birth to seven” (1 Samuel 2:5).
passages.later:
Mary's song echoes the same truth: God lifts the lowly. She sang that God “has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52).

Paul wrote that Christ, though equal with God, “humbled Himself and became obedient to death” (Philippians 2:8). The God of Psalm 113 who stoops to look at the earth came all the way down.

On the night he was arrested, after the Passover meal, Jesus and his disciples sang. “And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26:30). Many think they sang the end of the Hallel.
passages.hard: A word of care. Verse 9 praises God for giving a child to a woman who had none. It does not promise a child to every woman who prays for one. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. The note on Psalms 127 and 128 says more.
passages.asks:
Who is like the LORD? He is higher than anyone, and he bends lower than anyone. He notices the person at the dump and the woman crying at home.

Where do you look for greatness? Psalm 113 says God's greatness is shown in his care for the lowly. Ask who is on the dump in your town, and whether you are willing to stoop with him.
